statistical-question.recognize.root_reason: Telling a question answered by varying data from a question with one fixed answer uses only everyday asking and answering about groups; no earlier skill in the map supplies it.

edges.why: The statement defines a distribution as the values of a data set collected to answer a statistical question, so the learner must know what that question is.
The test problem gives the data as a dot plot, so the learner reads the dots as values before describing center, spread, and shape.
Symmetric and skewed name kinds of the overall shape of a distribution, described about its center and spread as first described informally.
A symmetric distribution has two sides about the center that are close to mirror images, which is the matching-halves idea of a line of symmetry.
The test problem shows each distribution as a dot plot on a scale, so the learner reads where dots pile up and where they trail off.
A measure of center puts into one number where a distribution's values center, and the test separates it from the range and spread named in the informal description.
A measure of variation puts into one number the informal spread of a distribution, how far apart its values lie, which the informal description first names.
A dot plot places each value at its mark on a number line, so the learner must locate whole-number values by their positions on the line.
A value occurs as many times as there are dots above it, so the learner counts the dots over each mark to list that value that many times.
Choosing equal-width intervals means adding the same width again and again to get each boundary, such as 10, 20, 30, and 40.
Placing each value in its interval means deciding which boundaries it is at least as great as and less than, including values that sit on a boundary.
Counting the values in each interval treats every interval as a category and counts the data values that fall in each one.
The horizontal axis is a number line marked at equally spaced interval boundaries, so whole numbers must be placed at their lengths from 0.
Each histogram bar is drawn up to its count on a vertical scale, the way a bar graph bar is drawn, here with no gaps between bars.
A histogram bar's count is read against the vertical scale just as a bar graph category count is read, giving how many values lie in the interval.
The bars stand over intervals marked on a number line axis, so interval ends such as 20 to under 30 are read as positions on that line.
The learner draws a number line whose scale covers the minimum and maximum and marks the five summary values at their positions on it.
The line across the box marks the median of the data set, so the learner must know what the median of a data set is.
The box runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile, so the learner must know what those two quartiles of a data set are.
Each summary value is read at its position on the number line under the box plot, so whole numbers must be read from marks on the line.
The line inside the box is read as the median, so the learner must know what the median of a data set is.
The ends of the box are read as the lower and upper quartiles, so the learner must know what those quartiles of a data set are.
The number of observations is found by counting the recorded values to find how many, counting a value again each time it occurs.
Naming the attribute measured on each individual uses the idea that one object has several measurable attributes and one of them is chosen.
Stating the unit of measurement uses the idea that a measurement is a number of standard units, as when a length is read in inches or centimeters.
Step 1 adds all the values of the data set, repeats included, and the test sum of five values stays within 100; any method of adding will do.
Step 2 counts the number of values in the data set, counting a repeated value each time it occurs, which is the number of observations.
Step 3 divides the sum by the number of values, and the test problem divides 40 by 5; any method of dividing will do.
Step 1 lists the values from least to greatest, which means deciding which of two values is greater, as with 9, 3, 7, 12, 5, and 10.
Step 2 depends on how many values are listed, repeated values included, so the learner counts the observations to find the middle.
Steps 2 and 3 branch on whether the number of values is odd or even, which is whether pairing the values leaves one over.
For an even number of values, step 3 takes the number halfway between the two middle values, such as the number halfway between 7 and 9.
Each quartile is defined as the median of a half of the ordered data, and step 1 finds the median of the whole set to split it.
The IQR is defined as the upper quartile minus the lower quartile, so the learner must know what the two quartiles of a data set are.
Step 2 subtracts the lower quartile from the upper quartile, such as 20 minus 12 in the test problem; any method of subtracting will do.
Step 1 finds the mean of the data set, and step 3 finds the mean of the distances, so the mean procedure is used twice.
The MAD averages the distances of values from the mean, and a distance between two numbers is the gap between them on a number line.
Step 2 subtracts the smaller number from the larger for each value and the mean, as in 5 minus 2 and 8 minus 5 in the test problem.
The overall pattern of where values lie, clusters, and gaps extends the description of a distribution by its center, spread, and shape.
A reason for a striking deviation comes from how the data were gathered and measured, which is the attribute, method, and unit of the data.
The explanation that the mean moves because every value enters the sum uses the definition of the mean as the sum divided by the number of values.
The explanation that the median barely moves uses its definition as the middle value of the ordered list, which depends only on position.
The reason the median describes a typical value better with outliers is that an extreme value pulls the mean but barely moves the median.
The choice depends on whether the distribution is roughly symmetric or strongly skewed, so the learner must recognize those shapes.
The statement separates distributions without outliers from those with outliers, so the learner must recognize values that depart strikingly from the pattern.
The test problem asks which measure better describes a typical house, which is judging a measure of center as one typical value.
One of the two measures being chosen between is the IQR, so the learner must know it as the interval holding the middle half of the data.
The other measure being chosen between is the MAD, and the reason extreme values inflate it comes from averaging distances from the mean.
The choice depends on whether the distribution is strongly skewed or roughly symmetric, so the learner must recognize those shapes.
The statement separates distributions with outliers from those without, so the learner must recognize values that depart strikingly from the pattern.
The IQR is reported with the median and the MAD with the mean, so the learner must know which center fits which distribution.
Interpreting the MAD as a typical distance from the mean uses its definition as the mean of the distances of the values from the mean.
A small MAD meaning values close to the mean and a larger MAD meaning values farther away applies the idea of a measure of variation.
The population is defined as the whole group a statistical question is about, so the learner must know what a statistical question asks about.
A representative sample is one that is like the population for the characteristic studied, so the learner must know the sample and the population.
A random sample is a sample chosen so that every member of the population has the same chance, so the learner must know sample and population.
The explanation that no part of the population is favored is that every member has the same chance of being chosen.
The claim is that random samples tend to be representative, so the learner must know what a representative sample is and why it supports valid conclusions.
A sample statistic is computed from a sample and estimates the matching statistic of the population, so the learner must know sample and population.
The test problem compares two sample means with the population mean, so the learner must know the mean of a data set as the statistic computed.
Step 1 draws several random samples of the same size, so the learner must know what makes a sample random.
Step 2 computes the mean of each sample drawn, such as the mean word length of 10 words.
Step 3 finds how far apart the least and greatest sample means are, which is the difference of the two numbers.
The test sample means 4.1, 4.8, 4.4, and 4.7 are decimals, so finding how far apart the least and greatest are subtracts decimals.
Step 4 uses how far sample means differ as the likely error of one sample mean, which rests on samples giving different values.
The statement gauges how far one sample mean, used as an estimate of the population mean, might be from that population mean.
Step 1 draws several random samples of the same size, so the learner must know what makes a sample random.
Step 2 writes the fraction of each sample in the category of interest, such as 11 of 20 voters, as a fraction of the sample.
Step 3 finds the least and greatest sample proportions, and samples of equal size give fractions with the same denominator to compare.
Step 3 finds how far apart the least and greatest proportions are, a difference of fractions with the same denominator such as 13/20 minus 9/20.
Step 4 uses how far sample proportions differ as the likely error of one sample proportion, which rests on samples giving different values.
The statement gauges how far one sample proportion, used as an estimate of the population proportion, might be from that population proportion.
Using the sample mean as an estimate of the unknown population mean applies the idea that a sample statistic estimates the matching population statistic.
The test problem finds the sample mean of the five word lengths 3, 5, 4, 6, and 7 before using it as the estimate.
The sample mean is a reasonable estimate only when the data come from a random sample, which tends to be representative of the population.
Using the sample fraction as an estimate of the unknown population fraction applies the idea that a sample statistic estimates the matching population statistic.
The test problem writes 30 of the 50 sampled students as the fraction 30/50 before using it as the estimate.
The sample fraction is a reasonable estimate only when the data come from a random sample, which tends to be representative of the population.
Comparing the centers of two distributions against their spread uses the informal description of each distribution by its center and spread.
The test problem shows each group as a dot plot on one shared scale, so the learner reads where each plot starts and ends.
The quantity compared is the difference between the centers of the two distributions, so the learner must know a center as one typical value.
The difference is measured in units of a common measure of variability such as the MAD, so the learner must know what such a measure is.
Step 1 subtracts the smaller center from the larger center, such as 190 minus 180 in the test problem; any method of subtracting will do.
Step 2 divides the difference by the common measure of variability, such as 10 divided by 5 in the test problem.
Step 3 reports how many measures of variability fit in the difference, which is a quotient read as the number of equal groups.
Judging the difference between centers against the variability means expressing that difference as a number of measures of variability.
Deciding that one population is generally greater uses the idea that distributions with little overlap relative to their spread are clearly separated.
The centers of the random samples are used as estimates of the centers of the two populations being compared.
The test problem gives each sample's variability as a MAD and asks for an explanation, so the learner reads a MAD as typical distance from the mean.
